newsitem.title: FRANCE: France pays heavily for insurer's "grim adventure".
newsitem.headline: France pays heavily for insurer's "grim adventure".

text.p: The French government revealed yet another tale of strategic error and corporate mismanagement on Thursday when it stepped in to pay a bill of 20 billion francs to rescue troubled state-controlled insurer GAN .

Lamenting another "grim adventure for the state-administered economy," Finance Minister Jean Arthuis said that the government would spend up to 20 billion francs to set Groupe des Assurances Nationales back on its feet and privatise it later this year.

GAN ran up 35 billion francs in losses since 1992 and it was time to seal off the "diseased" property business which had been dragging viable insurance and banking businesses down since the collapse of the French property market in the early 1990s.

The losses surpass those of state-owned bank Credit Lyonnais and home loans group Credit Foncier , two companies whose misadventures have been blamed in part on poor government supervision and led to costly government fix-ups.

Arthuis said those responsible for GAN's unbridled expansion at the height of a 1980s property boom and a costly strategy of cutting prices to conquer a bigger share of the insurance market had now left, but acknowledged that responsibility also lay with state officials for failing to address the trouble earlier.
The government already injected 2.8 billion francs into GAN last year but Arthuis said this state aid had been based on an "optimistic" assessment of the insurer's troubles.

The cost now was a far heftier state aid package, 11 billion francs in a capital injection this year, seven billion of it to shore up the accounts of a "diseased" property arm called UIC and 3.9 billion for the insurance division.

Another nine billion francs could be needed to cover the expected losses on bad loans to property developers and the sell-off of properties, although the money from privatisation could be used to reduce the burden on the state, he said.
"Our objective now is to insulate the insurance and banking side of the business to prevent contamination from a diseased property business," Arthuis told a news conference.
He said GAN Assurances and the profitable banking subsidiary Credit Industriel et Commercial were "nice businesses" which he wanted to privatise "during the course of 1997."
Ministry officials said the plan was still to privatise the two separately but that a sale in one go was not totally ruled out if investors declared an interest in such an operation.

The plan would leave the GAN holding company with UIC and two property defeasance structures, which the government said would have proved too costly to liquidate, and push the rest, if all goes according to plan, into the private sector.

GAN, whose board met on Thursday, said an audit commissioned by the government had reassed the price which property sell-offs and bad loans would cost and that UIC will as a result have cost GAN 30 billion francs in the three years since it took it over.

It also said GAN expected to report a net attributable loss of five billion francs for 1996, after a loss of 1.79 billion francs in 1995 and of 5.34 billion francs the previous year. UIC's losses for 1996 are expected to total 7.9 billion francs.
As in the case of Foncier and Credit Lyonnais, Arthuis said there could be legal proceedings if GAN boss Didier Pfeiffer wanted to establish who was to blame for GAN's difficulties.
He said it would seek approval for the aid package from the European Commission in Brussels, which controls state aid in the European Union.
But he underlined that the rescue would have no impact on the state budget and ministry officials said the money for the bailout would come from other privatisation proceeds.

GAN's former chairman, Jean-Jacques Bonnaud, who worked for the group for more than a decade, was fired by government in November, shortly after Arthuis cancelled a tender to privatise the CIC bank, blaming Bonnaud for failing to promote the sale.
